title: The tongue (James 3:1–12)
hook: a small rudder, a small spark: the tongue sets forests on fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith and works, and your line was faith that works. Which kind word did you turn into a done thing? Day six hundred seventy-four.

A wildfire can start from almost nothing. A spark from a dragged chain. One cigarette. A campfire left smoldering. A few days later the smoke is visible from space, and whole towns are packing their cars. Investigators sometimes trace the fire back to a single point on the ground, small enough to cover with your hand. James never saw a satellite photo, but he knew dry hillsides and summer fires. And he used them to describe something we all carry around, and use, several thousand times a day.

He starts with a warning to teachers. Not many of you should become teachers, he says, because teachers will be judged more strictly. People who talk for a living have more to answer for. Then three pictures of small things steering big ones. A bit in a horse's mouth turns the whole animal. A huge ship, driven by fierce winds, is "turned about with a very small helm," the rudder, wherever the pilot wants. And then the third: "Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!" That word matter in the King James is a bit of a puzzle in English. The Greek word means wood, or forest. How great a forest a small fire sets ablaze. The bit and the rudder steer. The spark destroys. Then James says something that stings: people have tamed every kind of animal, birds and snakes and sea creatures, "But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison." And here's the line that turns it inward. "Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be." We praise God with our mouths on Sunday and curse people made in God's likeness on Monday. James asks: does a spring pour out fresh water and bitter from the same opening? Can a fig tree grow olives? He isn't saying never speak. He's saying words are fire. They can warm a house or burn it down, and the same mouth does both.
screen: then, large: `HOW GREAT A MATTER A LITTLE FIRE KINDLETH!`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say no unkind word today. Settle, and breathe. Think back to the last unkind thing you said, out loud or in a text. Don't punish yourself; just look at it. Where did it go? Who heard it, and who did they tell? Picture it like a spark landing in dry grass. Now picture today. Where are you most likely to say something sharp? With whom? Picture that moment and your mouth staying closed, or opening with something else. A breath first. If you pray, you can ask for a guard on your mouth. The bell holds the time.
The tongue. For James, a small part of the body that steers like a rudder and burns like a spark, and that no one can fully tame.
Your line: a small fire. Today, before you send any message written in irritation, wait ten minutes, then reread it as the person getting it. Day six hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Many Christians examine their speech as part of daily or weekly self-examination, and James 3 is often read in churches when teaching about gossip, anger and online behavior.

original.note: Greek: tongue, and also language. the root of the English words gloss and glossary.

trapdoor: what it means: words are small and powerful, steering lives like rudders and burning them like sparks.
what a scholar hears: hylē, wood or forest, behind the KJV's 'matter', and a ladder of images, bit, rudder, spark, common in the ancient moral writers.

notes: ὕλη (3:5), KJV 'matter', as wood/forest: standard; confirm.
The bit/rudder/fire images have parallels in Greek moral writers (e.g. Plutarch, Philo); the trapdoor says 'common in the ancient moral writers'. Confirm or soften.
γλῶσσα and English 'gloss/glossary': standard etymology. Confirm.
The practice mentions 'a guard on your mouth' as a description (cf. Psalm 141:3), not a quotation.
